title: Tunnel Diodes, RTDs and Tunnel Transistors

questions.q: A tunnel diode is a p–n junction doped about a thousand times more heavily than usual. What two things does the heavy doping do?
options: It shrinks the depletion region to about 10 nm, and pushes the Fermi level into the bands
It widens the depletion region, so the junction blocks current better in both directions
It raises the band gap, and makes the junction a better insulator
It makes the junction transparent to light, and lets it glow when current flows
questions.explain: Very heavy doping (10¹⁹–10²⁰ cm⁻³) makes the depletion region, the wall, only about 10 nm thick, thin enough to tunnel through. It also moves the Fermi level into the bands, giving filled states on the n side that can face empty states on the p side.

questions.q: What rule decides whether an electron can tunnel across a tunnel diode's junction?
options: It keeps its energy, so it needs an empty state at the same energy on the other side
It must gain extra energy from the voltage before it can tunnel
It can tunnel only if the other side has no electrons at all
It can tunnel only when the junction is reverse-biased
questions.explain: Tunnelling keeps the electron's energy, so it can only tunnel into an empty state at the same energy opposite. The current flows when filled states face empty ones.

questions.q: The graph shows a tunnel diode's current (solid) and the three parts that add up to it (dashed and dotted). Why does the current not fall to zero in the valley?
questions.alt: Current against voltage: a solid curve rises to a peak near 0.07 V, falls through a shaded region to a valley near 0.33 V, then rises steeply; dashed and dotted curves labelled tunnelling, ordinary diode and excess (defects) show its three parts
options: The excess current through defect states, with the tail of the tunnelling current, fills it in
The ordinary diode current has already reached its full value there
The tunnelling current stays at about a fifth of its peak, whatever the voltage
Heat left over from the peak keeps a little current flowing through the junction
questions.explain: Three currents add up: tunnelling makes the first hump, the ordinary diode current makes the final rise, and a small excess current through defect states fills the valley. The peak-to-valley current ratio (about 5.6 here) is the tunnel diode's figure of merit.

questions.q: The graph shows a tunnel diode's current against voltage. In the shaded region more voltage gives less current. Does the diode produce power there?
questions.alt: Current against voltage: the current rises to a peak near 0.07 V, falls through a shaded region to a valley near 0.33 V, then rises steeply; dashed curves show the tunnelling, ordinary-diode and defect currents
options: No: current and voltage are still both positive, so it still absorbs power
Yes: its resistance is negative there, so it gives out power like a battery
Yes, but only at the valley, where the current is smallest
No: no current flows at all in the shaded region
questions.explain: 'Negative differential resistance' means that the change in voltage divided by the change in current is negative. Current and voltage themselves are both positive, so the diode still absorbs power: only the changes have opposite signs.

questions.q: How can a tunnel diode be used to make an oscillator?
options: Biased in its falling region, it cancels a resonant circuit's losses, so the oscillation keeps going
It switches on and off by itself at its peak current, like a clock, with no other parts
It stores charge at the valley and releases it at the peak, giving pulses of current
It converts heat into an alternating current at its own natural frequency
questions.explain: A resonant circuit rings and dies away because of its losses. Biased in its falling (negative-resistance) region, a tunnel diode cancels those losses, so the oscillation grows and then keeps going.

questions.q: A resonant-tunnelling diode has two thin walls with a quantum well between them. Why can an electron at one particular energy pass through both walls almost every time?
options: At the well's level the reflections from the two walls cancel, so the electron is hardly reflected at all
At that energy the electron has enough energy to go over both walls
At that energy the two walls become thinner and let the electron through
At that energy the electron loses its charge and is no longer stopped by the walls
questions.explain: At the energy of the well's level the waves reflected from the two walls cancel, and the electron passes almost every time. At other energies it is almost always reflected: a sharp energy filter.

questions.q: The graph shows a resonant-tunnelling diode's current against voltage. The voltage pulls the well's level down. Why does the current fall after the peak (b)?
questions.alt: Current against voltage from 0 to 0.4 V: the current rises through point a to a sharp peak b near 0.13 V, falls to a valley c near 0.25 V, then rises again
options: The level has dropped below the incoming electrons' band, so no electron has the right energy to pass
The level has risen far above the incoming electrons, so they have too little energy to pass
The two walls have melted together, so the well has disappeared
The electrons have filled the well, so no more can get in
questions.explain: (a) The level is above the electrons: little current. (b) It lines up with them: resonance and the peak. (c) It has dropped below the emitter's band, so nothing has the right energy and the current falls.

questions.q: Why can an ordinary MOSFET not switch more steeply than about 60 mV per tenfold change in current at room temperature?
options: When it is off, only the few 'hot' electrons with enough energy get over the barrier, and their number falls only so fast
Its source and drain contacts have too much resistance for a faster switch
Its channel is too long for the electrons to reach the drain quickly
Its electrons tunnel through the gate oxide and cancel part of the gate voltage
questions.explain: A MOSFET lets electrons over a barrier set by the gate. When it is meant to be off, only the hot tail of electrons gets over, and that tail sets the 60 mV per decade limit: it is set by temperature, not by the oxide or the contacts. So supply voltages have hardly fallen in twenty years.

questions.q: The picture compares a MOSFET with a tunnel FET. How does the tunnel FET try to switch more steeply than 60 mV per decade?
questions.alt: Left: energy bands of a MOSFET with an n-type source. Middle: energy bands of a tunnel FET with a p+ source. Right: illustrative switching curves for the two
options: Electrons tunnel in from the source's valence band, which cuts off the hot tail of electrons
Its gate oxide is thinner, so the gate pulls the channel's bands down harder
Its channel is shorter, so electrons cross before they have time to scatter
Its source is more heavily doped, so more hot electrons get over the barrier
questions.explain: In a tunnel FET the source is p-type. The gate pulls the channel's band below the source's filled valence band, opening a window. Electrons above the top of the valence band have nothing to tunnel into, so the hot tail is cut off and switching can be steeper.

questions.q: True or false: tunnel FETs are already used in mainstream computer chips.
options: True
False
questions.explain: False. Laboratory tunnel FETs beat 60 mV per decade, usually only at very low currents, but tunnelling passes far fewer electrons than going over a barrier, so circuits would be slow. They remain research in 2026.
